reason: The sources provide 21 highly detailed, overlapping claims with direct quotes confirming the timeline, key historical figures, destruction metrics, and the scapegoating of Robert Hubert.
story: In September 1666, London was a sprawling timber metropolis of over 300,000 people. Shortly after midnight on Sunday, September 2, a spark in Thomas Farriner’s Pudding Lane bakery ignited a catastrophe. Fueled by a fierce eastern gale and delayed by the indecision of Lord Mayor Sir Thomas Bloodworth, the flames grew into a firestorm. The family fled through a window, but their terrified maid stayed behind, becoming the first of only six officially recorded victims. Diarist Samuel Pepys recorded the horrors as the fire consumed over 13,000 houses, 80 churches, the Royal Exchange, and Old St. Paul’s Cathedral. To halt the destruction, buildings were demolished to create firebreaks. Amidst the chaos, a Second Anglo-Dutch War fueled mass paranoia, prompting the wrongful hanging of a simple-minded Frenchman, Robert Hubert. Rebuilding began under a February 1667 Act, banning timber exteriors and reshaping London under architect Sir Christopher Wren.
angle: Despite consuming over 13,000 homes, 80 churches, and Old St. Paul's Cathedral, the Great Fire of London officially claimed only six recorded lives, while a completely innocent Frenchman was hanged as a scapegoat.

claims.claim: The Great Fire of London occurred from September 2 to September 5, 1666.

evidence.quote: The Great Fire of London occurred from Sunday 2 September to Wednesday 5 September 1666, gutting the medieval City of London inside the old Roman city wall, while also extending past the wall to the west.
The small blaze spread between September 2 and 5 1666, leaving 436 acres of the city completely destroyed.

claims.claim: The fire started in a bakery in Pudding Lane.

evidence.quote: The fire started in a bakery in Pudding Lane shortly after midnight on Sunday 2 September and spread rapidly.
It started in a baker’s shop in Pudding Lane, to the north of London Bridge.

claims.claim: The bakery where the fire began was owned by Thomas Farriner.

evidence.quote: A short time after midnight on Sunday, 2 September 1666, a fire broke out at Thomas Farriner's bakery in Pudding Lane.
The shop where the fire is believed to have begun was that of Thomas Farriner, King Charles II's baker.

claims.claim: Sir Thomas Bloodworth was the Lord Mayor of London during the fire.

evidence.quote: The Lord Mayor, Sir Thomas Bloodworth, hesitated in giving the order to employ this method.
Pepys blamed the length of time taken to put the fire out on the lord mayor at the time, Sir Thomas Bloodworth, for not doing enough to stop the fire spreading.

claims.claim: A maidservant at the bakery was too afraid to escape the fire and died.

evidence.quote: The occupants, save the family's maidservant, who was too frightened to try, fled through an upstairs window to the house next door. When the house burned down, she became the fire's first victim.
When the house caught fire, all of the family jumped out the window to save themselves, except the maid who was too afraid. She was one of the few victims claimed by the fire.

claims.claim: Samuel Pepys was a diarist who recorded the fire.

evidence.quote: The day the great fire began on 2 September 1666, the diarist Samuel Pepys took to the safety of the south side of the river Thames and watched the flames gradually consume London’s medieval city.
The famous diarist Samuel Pepys provides the best recorded account of the tragedy.

claims.claim: King Charles II was the ruler of England during the fire.

evidence.quote: Tuesday, the fire spread over nearly the whole city, destroying Old St Paul's Cathedral and leaping the River Fleet to threaten Charles II's court at Whitehall Palace.
However, the idea has also been attributed to the Stuart king at the time, Charles II, who took a lead role in the attempt to save the city.

claims.claim: A strong east wind fueled and propelled the flames across the city.

evidence.quote: The battle to put out the fire is considered to have been won by two key factors: the strong east wind dropped, and the Tower of London garrison used gunpowder to create effective firebreaks, halting further spread eastward.
To compound the issue, a strong wind from the east propelled the flames across the city.

claims.claim: Demolishing buildings in the fire's path to create firebreaks was a primary firefighting technique.

evidence.quote: The main firefighting technique of the time was the creation of firebreaks by means of removing structures in the fire's path.
This may have been down to the quick thinking of Pepys, who has been credited with the idea of destroying buildings on the fire's path to impede its progress.

claims.claim: Old St. Paul's Cathedral was destroyed by the fire.

evidence.quote: On Tuesday, the fire spread over nearly the whole city, destroying Old St Paul's Cathedral and leaping the River Fleet to threaten Charles II's court at Whitehall Palace.

Within hours it was beyond control and by the time it was finally checked it had destroyed an estimated 13,000 houses, 87 of the 109 parish churches, 43 Livery Halls, the Royal Exchange, as well as St Paul's Cathedral.

claims.claim: The Royal Exchange was destroyed in the Great Fire.

evidence.quote: The Royal Exchange caught fire in the late afternoon, and was a "smoking shell" within a few hours.

Within hours it was beyond control and by the time it was finally checked it had destroyed an estimated 13,000 houses, 87 of the 109 parish churches, 43 Livery Halls, the Royal Exchange, as well as St Paul's Cathedral.

claims.claim: The traditional number of recorded deaths from the fire is six.

evidence.quote: Field argues that the number "may have been higher than the traditional figure of six, but it is likely it did not run into the hundreds"
Though around 13,200 houses and 84 churches were destroyed, only six people are known to have died.

claims.claim: Sir Christopher Wren was the architect responsible for St. Paul's Cathedral.

evidence.quote: Christopher Wren, of course, would get his defining masterpiece: St Paul’s Cathedral, declared complete in 1711.
The architect Sir Christopher Wren oversaw a huge rebuilding project to restore the city, including the reconstruction of St Paul's cathedral, an iconic part of London's skyline to this day.

claims.claim: The Rebuilding Act passed in February 1667 banned the use of timber for building exteriors.

evidence.quote: In February 1667, a Fire Court began sorting out remaining disputes, and the Rebuilding Act was passed to regulate the heights of new buildings (no more than four storeys) and the kinds of materials used (timber exteriors were banned, for obvious reasons).
While it is true that the February 1667 Rebuilding Act stated that ‘all the outsides of all Buildings in and about the said Citty be henceforth made of Bricke or Stone’

claims.claim: A previous major fire had occurred on London Bridge in 1633.

evidence.quote: London Bridge, the only physical connection between the City and the south side of the river Thames, had been noted as a deathtrap in the fire of 1633.

An earlier seventeenth century fire, which destroyed many houses on London Bridge in 1633, was chronicled by Nehemiah Wallington (1598-1658), a puritan turner who lived in the parish of St Leonard Eastcheap with his wife Grace and their five children, four of whom died in infancy.

claims.claim: A special Fire Court was established in February 1667 to settle rebuild disputes.

evidence.quote: A special Fire Court was set up from February 1667 to December 1668, and again from 1670 to February 1676.

In February 1667, a Fire Court began sorting out remaining disputes, and the Rebuilding Act was passed to regulate the heights of new buildings (no more than four storeys) and the kinds of materials used (timber exteriors were banned, for obvious reasons).

claims.claim: The ongoing war fueled suspicion that French and Dutch foreign enemies had set the fire.

evidence.quote: The fears of the homeless focused on the French and Dutch, England's enemies in the ongoing Second Anglo-Dutch War; these substantial immigrant groups became victims of street violence.
As England was at war with France and the Netherlands, there was also suspicion that foreign enemies were behind the tragedy.

disputed: The true death toll of the fire: S1 notes that while the official/traditional toll is six or eight, historians like Hanson argue it could have been hundreds or thousands due to cremation of bodies in intense heat and subsequent winter exposure. The script should mention the traditional single-digit count but note the likely higher undocumented toll.

Whether the fire ended the Great Plague: S4 suggests the fire wiped out the filthy areas of the plague, while S5 strongly disputes this as a common myth since the fire only burned a quarter of the metropolis. The script must treat this as a myth.

Who first suggested creating firebreaks: S4 credits Pepys with the idea of blowing up buildings, while also noting it has been attributed to King Charles II. The script should attribute this action generally to both Pepys and the royal authorities.
